audience.programmeDescription: Public Administration (Bestuurskunde) at Erasmus University Rotterdam examines how governments and public organizations address social problems. Students combine policy, politics, law, sociology, economics and management with social research, a public-sector internship and a bachelor project. The selected programme is the Dutch-language full-time bachelor.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR option combines politics, law, economics, sociology and public-policy analysis; the second adds a substantial climate and sustainability focus. Neither reproduces EUR’s dedicated public-administration degree. Its integrated public-administration sequence, required internship and bachelor-project sequence remain important differences. Shared rows show content relationships, including partial matches, rather than course equivalence.

curriculum.limitation: The complete EUR curriculum comprises 180 EC over three years, including a 15-EC approved minor. Some lectures are in English; the Dutch offering retains Dutch working groups, assignments and assessments.

componentNotes.pa-minor: 15 EC of approved minor study; its subject is not fixed in this comparison.
componentNotes.pa-internship: Required 15-EC public-sector placement; the programme describes ten weeks of practical experience.
componentNotes.pa-bachelor-project: Required 15-EC public-administration research project. This differs from optional UCR research outside the 180 EC.

concepts.concept: Politics, law, sociology and economics provide different ways to examine public institutions and policy choices. Research methods, ethics, organizational psychology and leadership connect those perspectives to public problems. This is an interdisciplinary UCR response, with gaps in dedicated public-administration teaching and compulsory professional practice.
concepts.labelRationale: The completed curriculum combines political science, constitutional/international/EU law, sociology, economics, methods and organisational study. The label names its academic substance and does not imply a UCR public-administration qualification.

concepts.concept: Public institutions and policy are studied alongside climate change, water management, environmental justice and resource stewardship. Science and laboratory study support informed analysis of sustainability choices. The programme combines governance with environmental knowledge; it is not a specialist public-administration or environmental-engineering degree.
basisLabels: How should governments govern climate and sustainability challenges?
concepts.labelRationale: The visible label was reviewed after completion of the 24-course curriculum and describes its substantive organising direction without treating the generating concept as an official UCR track or overstating one strand of the programme.
concepts.distinctnessRationale: Compared with the closest match, this route replaces seven courses (52.5 EC) with sustainability and environmental-governance study. The changed courses are consequences of the evidenced climate-policy direction, not threshold-filling substitutions.

notes.text: EUR combines public-administration theory and policy analysis with law, economics, sociology, management, a required public-sector internship and a bachelor project. UCR offers related interdisciplinary study, with a second option focused on sustainability governance. It does not reproduce the dedicated policy, internship and bachelor-project sequence. Shared rows include partial content relationships; blank cells show deliberate gaps. Optional independent research is additional to the displayed 180 EC.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourseDescriptions.description: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

courseEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Introduction to Economics
selectedCourseDescriptions.description: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

courseEvidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.

Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.

Algebraic and graphical analysis and interpretation of macroeconomic indicators support the evaluation of economic developments and fiscal and monetary policy.

Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Econometrics
selectedCourseDescriptions.description: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

selectedCourseDescriptions.description: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership in diverse contexts, with particular attention to minority experiences. Students design and pilot a quantitative survey, collect data ethically, and use SPSS or RStudio for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression. They interpret the findings and develop evidence-based leadership recommendations.

courseEvidence.profile: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, emotional expression and suppression, emotional labor, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership and social interaction under conflict, exclusion and interpersonal uncertainty. It emphasises inclusive leadership and ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences, with digital emotion regulation as a further strand. Students conduct a supervised quantitative survey project: formulating theory-driven hypotheses, selecting established psychological measures, designing and piloting a Qualtrics survey, recruiting participants ethically, collecting original data and preparing a clean dataset. Individual work applies descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio, and interprets findings and limitations in empirical reports and evidence-based leadership recommendations.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseDescriptions.description: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
